references.text: Isaiah describes the same opponents who have a 'prostitute' as father and a 'deceiver' as mother, and who claim to have a covenant with death, paralleling Jesus' accusation that they have the devil as their father and refuse to believe in him.

Here the Lord calls Israel children who will not obey, and asks: 'Why do you fight against me?' This mirrors the dialogue in John 8 where Jesus confronts them with their rebellion against God's will and their claim to have God as their father.

Isaiah prays to God as 'father' and asks: 'Why do you let us stray from your ways?' This corresponds directly to the counterargument in John 8:41 where the opponents claim, 'We have one father, God,' even though their actions show disobedience.

John 1:12-13 describes those who become God's children not by 'blood' or 'the will of the flesh,' but by God. This is the theological opposite of the claim in John 8:41 to be born of a 'prostitute' (fleshly origin) while simultaneously claiming to have God as their father.

In the following verses, Jesus expands on the accusation by saying that their father is the devil and that they do the devil's desires. This is the direct continuation of the theme of 'fatherhood' and 'deeds' introduced in verse 41.

Paul refers to this conflict in John 8 by calling those under the law 'Hagar' (slaves) and those who are free 'Sarah' (free), and asks: 'What does Scripture say? That Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman.' This connects to the theme of origin and identity discussed in John 8.
